extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether additional claim elements 'integrate' a recited judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, product of nature) into a practical application such that the claim is not 'directed to' the exception. Covers considerations, examples, and procedural steps for examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature / markedly-different-characteristics requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of claimed subject matter that are innate to naturally occurring material and not markedly different from their natural counterparts render claims directed to a product of nature ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claimed characteristics are 'innate to naturally occurring DNA' or inherent to a natural material (e.g., ductility of vanadium, genetic sequence of DNA, cloned animal genetics), the claims lack 'markedly different characteristics' and are products of nature exceptions (citing Ambry Genetics, In re Marden, In re Roslin). Phenotypic or structural differences that are not claimed are irrelevant. The claimed features must themselves show the marked differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two) — general
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying a judicial exception (Step 2A Prong One), evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application; if so, the claim is not directed to the exception and is eligible at Pathway B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim 'integrates' a judicial exception when the additional elements apply, rely on, or use the exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the exception rather than merely attempting to monopolize it. The evaluation uses a set of considerations (non-exclusive) and follows the procedure of identifying additional elements and evaluating them individually and in combination (see MPEP § 2106.05 subsections for details). If integration is found, Step 2A concludes (Step 2A: NO). If not, proceed to Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement in the functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that demonstrates an improvement to computer functionality or another technology/technical field can show integration of the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consult the specification to determine whether disclosure provides sufficient detail for a person of ordinary skill to recognize the improvement; the specification need not explicitly say 'improvement' but must make it apparent. The claim must reflect the components/steps that provide the improvement (it need not recite the improvement in words). This 'improvements' consideration at Step 2A does not consider whether the elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional. Case examples: Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory, Finjan, SRI (see MPEP § 2106.05(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying or using the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that use the judicial exception to effect a particular medical treatment or prophylaxis can integrate the exception into a practical application and thus be not directed to the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration is distinct and elevated due to cases like Vanda. Claims that include administration/treatment steps that use a natural-law relationship to guide or limit therapy (e.g., genotype-guided dosing to reduce risk) may be eligible at Step 2A because the steps are directed to treating the patient, not merely gathering diagnostic data (contrast with Mayo). Examples of 'treatment' limitations include administration of medication, surgery, dialysis, physiotherapy, phototherapy, organ transplants, acupuncture, radiation therapy, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementing the judicial exception with, or using it in conjunction with, a particular machine or manufacture integral to the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that implements or uses the judicial exception with a specific machine or manufacture integral to the claim may indicate integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim recites a particular machine/manufacture that is integral (not merely a generic computer). Specificity of the machine-related limitations is relevant to determine if they meaningfully limit the exception (see MPEP §§ 2106.05(b),(f)). Mere recitation of a generic machine is insufficient; the claim should reflect how the machine is integral to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that effects a transformation (physical or functional) of an article to a different state or thing can show integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim limitations produce a transformation or reduction in an article such that the exception is applied in a meaningful technical manner. This consideration is discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(c). Physical steps alone are not automatically sufficient; the transformation must be meaningful in context of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying or using the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond a general field link
rubrics_metrics.description: Any additional elements that apply or use the judicial exception in a meaningful way beyond merely linking it to a technological environment can indicate integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a catch-all for limitations that impose meaningful limits on the exception beyond general field-of-use or environment links. The claim as a whole should be more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception (see MPEP § 2106.05(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Merely reciting application language or implementing on a computer (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely reciting 'apply it' (or equivalent), instructing implementation of an abstract idea on a computer, or merely using a computer as a tool to perform the abstract idea does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such recitations are treated as insignificant post-solution activity or generic computer implementation (see MPEP § 2106.05(f) and cases like Alice). Examiners should not treat the mere presence of routine computer implementation as meaningful limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant pre- or post-solution activity to the judicial exception does not integrate it into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations that are ancillary, conventional, or insignificant to the recited exception (insubstantial 'extra-solution' activity) should be treated as not imposing meaningful limits (see MPEP § 2106.05(g) and Parker v. Flook example where failure to describe specifics made additional steps insignificant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally linking the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use is insufficient (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that merely links the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General field-of-use limitations or merely stating the technological context without meaningful limiting interaction between the additional elements and the exception will not render the claim eligible (see MPEP § 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangibility/physicality is not a determinative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element is not a relevant consideration in Step 2A Prong Two; tangible implementation does not guarantee eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on 'physical' existence alone to find integration (Alice: the fact a computer exists is 'beside the point'). Conversely, non-physical elements do not doom eligibility (Enfish, McRO examples). Evaluate how elements meaningfully limit the exception rather than whether they are physical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of claimed limitations — not a standalone but relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific ways of achieving a result are not standalone considerations, but the specificity of claim limitations is relevant to evaluations of particular machine, transformation, and mere-instruction-to-apply considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that lack specificity about how to implement the additional elements (e.g., how to select parameters, monitor variables, or effect steps) may be found to recite only insignificant post-solution activity (see Parker v. Flook). Examiners should consider specificity when applying related considerations (MPEP §§ 2106.05(b),(c),(f)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of conventionality from Step 2A Prong Two analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2A Prong Two, examiners should not consider whether the additional elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity; all additional elements should be given weight regardless of conventionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike Step 2B, Step 2A focuses on whether additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application irrespective of whether those elements are conventional. Thus, conventional or routine activity may nonetheless integrate an exception at Prong Two and should not be disregarded on that basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural method for Prong Two evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate integration into a practical application, identify additional claim elements beyond the judicial exception and evaluate those elements individually and in combination using the listed considerations; not all considerations apply to every claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis is not a weighing test; the number or label of applicable considerations is immaterial. Focus on the significance of the additional elements relative to the applicant’s invention and whether they integrate the exception into a practical application. Examine each claim separately — claims in the same application may yield different eligibility outcomes. For multiple exceptions recited, see MPEP § 2106.04 subsection II.B.
